NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday described the protests against his predecessor, Mamata Banerjee , at Hailsahar in North 24 Parganas as a reflection of “strong public anger.”Mamata Banerjee faced protests earlier in the day when a group of protesters allegedly surrounded her vehicle, raised “chor-chor” (thief, thief) slogans and hurled mud and slippers at her car. She had gone to meet the family of a Trinamool Congress (TMC) worker who allegedly died in police custody.Denying any involvement of the ruling BJP in the incident, Adhikari said, “You (Mamata Banerjee) have committed so much theft, you will have to hear people call you a thief.”He further claimed that the TMC supremo went to Halisahar without being invited by the deceased’s family and that the TMC worker's family was "satisfied" with the police and administration.“Do not do this when the family is shutting the door. You are saying you will enter by force. Do it when people seek your help or intervention. This is the time for development. Do not go anywhere and do anything that disrupts normal life,” he added.The chief minister also questioned why his predecessor had not visited the family of “Abhaya” (fearless), the moniker given to the RG Kar rape and murder victim, on the second anniversary of her death.“You could have gone to Abhaya’s house today. You could have gone to Ratna Debnath with a towel around your neck and apologised, saying you had made a mistake and asking for forgiveness. I believe she would have forgiven you,” Adhikari remarked.Ratna Debnath, Abhaya’s mother, is now a BJP MLA. She had previously said she contested the recent West Bengal assembly elections to fight for justice and accused Mamata Banerjee, who was the chief minister at the time of the RG Kar incident, of failing to save "Abhaya."Meanwhile, Adhkari accused Mamata Banerjee of trying to sabotage probe into the RG Kar incident, and questioned why would people not be angry with her.He asked: “You (Banerjee) killed Abhaya, went to destroy evidence and tried to buy her family with Rs 10 lakh. If people threw mud at your car, what else would they throw? Flowers?”Earlier, Mamata Banerjee was forced to pass through a police cordon as the demonstration briefly turned the road into a charged political theatre, with rival sides trading allegations of conspiracy, provocation and administrative failure.“My car has been attacked with stones, shoes and mud. This is nothing but a conspiracy. I had informed the police that I would be coming, but despite that, no security measures were taken,” she told reporters after reaching the area.The former chief minister also alleged that "large bricks" had been thrown at her vehicle.“My head could have been smashed. I could have died here,” she claimed, accusing the BJP-led state government of using “goons” to target her.Mamata Banerjee also trained her guns on CM Adhikari, saying she had "no particular anger" against the police but alleging that the force was being used at the behest of the state government.“The police are protecting the lumpens. Bengal has fallen into the hands of lumpens,” she added, saying her party would pursue the matter.
Article Summary: Mamata Banerjee faced protests earlier in the day when a group of protesters allegedly surrounded her vehicle, raised “chor-chor” (thief, thief) slogans and hurled mud and slippers at her car. She had gone to meet the family of a Trinamool Congress (TMC) worker who allegedly died in police custody.

Article Title: ED director Rahul Navin gets 1-year extension
Article Text:
ED director Rahul Navin (File photo)

NEW DELHI: Rahul Navin gets one year extension as ED director. His 2-yr fixed tenure was coming to an end this month, now extended till 13 Aug 2027.According to a notification issued by the DoPT on Saturday, “Appointments Committee of the Cabinet has approved extension in tenure of Rahul Navin, IRS, as Director of Enforcement in the Directorate of Enforcement for a period of one year beyond 13.08.2026 i.e. up to 13.08.2027, including extension in service beyond the date of his superannuation i.e. 31.07.2027, or until further orders, whichever is earlier.”After three years as director ED, Navin, a 1993 batch officer of the Indian Revenue Service (Income Tax), stands a chance of getting two more extensions and serve till Aug 2029, all through the present tenure of the Modi govt with next general elections due in April-May 2029.As per service age Navin’s retirement is due on 31 July 2027, but tenure of ED director can continue beyond that as in the case of his predecessor Sanjay Mishra.Rahul Navin hails from Bihar and had an outstanding academic distinction with a degree in BTech and MTech from IIT Kanpurand an MBA from Swinburne University of Technology, Melbourne.On 15th September 2023, he assumed charge as Director (In-Charge) and was appointed as Director of ED on 14th August 2024.He has also written a book on "Information Exchange and Tax Transparency: Tackling Global Tax Evasion and Avoidance" while being in the tax policy division of the finance ministry.As ED director, Navin has laid down a new roadmap for his officers of completing all investigations within two years and ensuring attached properties are auctioned and restituted to the rightful claimant and victims of frauds — whether it be banks or individuals — within a specific timeframe.He has set a target for all the zonal offices for filing of chargesheets, minimizing avoidable delays.The ED has so far restored assets valued over Rs 35,000 crore to victims of fraud using the provision under sections 8(7) and 8(8) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), which allow for “the restoration of assets to rightful owners when it is determined that the properties were initially acquired through illicit means but legally belong to innocent parties”.
Article Summary: Rahul Navin gets one year extension as ED director. His 2-yr fixed tenure was coming to an end this month, now extended till 13 Aug 2027. After three years as director ED, Navin stands a chance of getting two more extensions and serve till Aug 2029.

Article Title: DGCA to conduct preliminary probe into Baramati aircraft runway excursion: Centre

(With PTI inputs)

NEW DELHI: The ministry of civil aviation (MoCA) said on Sunday that a team from aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), is being sent to Maharashtra’s Baramati airfield, where a Cessna training aircraft was involved in a runway excursion earlier in the day.“The air safety team from the DGCA is going to the site to conduct a preliminary investigation and ascertain the circumstances and contributing factors leading to the incident,” the ministry statement read.MoCA further noted that the plane appeared to have sustained damage to its propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear, while no fatalities or injuries were reported.“There were no injuries or fatalities reported. The aircraft has sustained prima facie damage to the propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear. A detailed assessment of the damage will be carried out by the competent authorities,” the statement added.According to the ministry, the incident occurred around 12:25 pm when the Cessna C172, bearing registration VT-SEX and operated by flying training school Academy of Carver Aviation, veered off the runway at Baramati airfield.The aircraft was being operated for a Circuit and Landing Emergencies (CL Emergencies) training exercise.It was under the command of flight instructor Captain Chirag Shashikant Doifode, with trainee Abhijeet Jundre on board.The plane had taxied out at around 12:09 pm for the scheduled training exercise.“During the exercise, the aircraft entered the runway through Link Bravo and lined up at the threshold of runway 29, where a rejected take-off exercise practice was carried out.“Subsequently, the aircraft lined up at the threshold of runway 11 and another rejected take-off exercise was carried out,” the statement noted.During the exercise, the aircraft was unable to stop within the paved runway surface and subsequently veered off the extended paved surface beyond the threshold of runway 29 towards the right side, resulting in a runway excursion, according to the ministry.
Article Summary: A team from aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), is being sent to Maharashtra’s Baramati airfield. A Cessna training aircraft was involved in a runway excursion earlier in the day. The plane appeared to have sustained damage to its propeller, engine cowling and nose landing gear.

TMC MPs Kalyan Banerjee and Dola Sen were accompanying her.Kalyan Banerjee described the incident as an "attempt to murder" and alleged that the attack was targeted at Mamata Banerjee. He also accused the police of remaining silent spectators while the incident took place."The entire car, there was not a single second when stones were not thrown. Stones were thrown every moment, targeting Mamata Banerjee to assault her," Kalyan Banerjee said, as cited by news agency ANI.He alleged that hundreds of BJP workers were present at the spot and claimed that the incident took place in the presence of police personnel."Hundreds and hundreds of BJP workers were there, and police were remaining silent spectators, absolutely silent spectators," he said.Kalyan Banerjee also alleged that there was a direction from West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari behind the incident."Of course there was a direction given by the CM Suvendu Adhikari," he said.TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee also accused the BJP of unleashing political violence in West Bengal and alleged that Mamata Banerjee was "brutally attacked" while travelling to meet the family of the deceased party worker.In a post on social media, Abhishek Banerjee alleged that the incident reflected a wider law-and-order failure in the state."And now, a former Chief Minister of the state, who was on her way to meet the grieving family, is brutally attacked by goons planted by BJP," he said, as reported by ANI.He questioned the police response and said the incident represented a "failure of governance"."This is not merely a failure of the state police. This is a failure of governance," Abhishek Banerjee said.He also alleged that the police had failed to protect TMC workers and the grieving family, and questioned whether political violence had become a tool of governance in the state.Rajya Sabha MP Dola Sen said Mamata Banerjee had gone to meet the family of the TMC worker who allegedly died in police custody and questioned whether she should have been prevented from making the visit."Our worker died in police custody, an incident akin to a lockup death. His wife is a councillor. You tell me, as a matter of simple, natural justice, should our leader, Mamata Banerjee, not go to meet that family?" Sen said.She alleged that stones and half-bricks were thrown at Mamata Banerjee's vehicle and claimed that BJP workers and police personnel were present at the spot."They attacked her in a targeted manner... BJP goons and police stood in front, throwing half-bricks and stones, cracking the glass of Didi's car," she alleged.Sen also said Mamata Banerjee's visit was not a political programme but an attempt to meet the family of the deceased worker.Mamata Banerjee herself alleged that large stones were hurled at her car in front of police personnel and said the attack could have resulted in serious injuries or death."Large stones were hurled at my car by anti-social elements, right in front of the police. The attack on the vehicle was so severe that if the windows had been open, my head would have been split open. We could have all been killed," she said.She also alleged that the police were providing protection to the BJP and said she had never witnessed such an incident before."This happened right in front of the police. I have never seen anything like this. What is going on?" she said."Chor bhagao" slogans were also heard from the crowd, according to ANI.West Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya denied any BJP involvement in the alleged attack and condemned the throwing of stones or other objects at Mamata Banerjee's vehicle."Let me be clear: the BJP has absolutely no connection to the incidents where mud, stones, or slippers were thrown at Mamata Banerjee's vehicle," Bhattacharya said, according to ANI.He said the BJP did not endorse such behaviour and called for police action against those responsible."It is between the public and TMC," he said, while maintaining that the BJP condemned the incident.State minister Agnimitra Paul also condemned the alleged attack and said neither she nor the BJP supported such actions."Mamata Banerjee may have committed many wrongs or made many mistakes, but we can never support this kind of behaviour, especially against a woman, and an elderly woman. We do not endorse this. If anyone is carrying out such acts while claiming to represent the BJP, they are in the wrong," Paul said.
Article Summary: Mamata Banerjee was on her way to meet the family of a TMC worker who allegedly died in police custody when the incident took place. TMC MPs Kalyan Banerzee and Dola Sen were accompanying her. They have accused the BJP of being behind the alleged attack.

Article Title: The women who paint Jharkhand: Sohrai-Khovar's journey from ritual to global gallery
Article Text:
Sohrai-Khovar, an ancient women-led art tradition from Jharkhand (Image: TWAC)

What is Sohrai-Khovar?

Ganju Sohrai painted house (Source: TWAC)

Inside of a Khovar room (Source: TWAC)

From mud walls to airport terminals

Painting gifted to Russian President Putin by PM Modi

Tensions surrounding the craft

Gangwa's Lotus - archival art (Source: TWAC)

Pashupati by Kunti Devi (Source: TWAC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A local artisan crouches by her doorstep, her hands stained with mud and colour drawn straight from the earth around her. The warmth of rust red, the hush of chalky white, the depth of a black gone nearly charcoal. With nothing more than a broken comb and a steady hand, she draws a peacock on a wall still damp from its coating of clay. In a few hours, this wall, like thousands of others across Hazaribagh, will carry the story of the land of Jharkhand, a mural to its beauty.Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. In 1991, celebrated and renowned environmentalist Bulu Imam documented rock shelters in the Isco hills of Hazaribagh district and noticed that the motifs on the ancient cave walls closely resembled the paintings still being made on village homes nearbyImam was able to sketch out a connection between the 21st century walls of a home to the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic caves of 10,000 to 5,000 BCE. Other researchers, citing the Archaeological Survey of India, place the rock art closer to 7,000-4,000 BCE, in the Paleolithic period.The dates might be contested but what remains true is that Sohrai and Khovar painting represent one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent, a line running from cave wall to mud wall across several thousand years.Sohrai was originally a season specific craft style painted around the harvest festival of the same name, celebrated after Diwali in the month of Kartik, when households give thanks to their cattle and to the land.Khovar, the word draws from "kho," meaning cave, and "var," meaning groom, is painted for weddings, decorating the room where a newly married couple will spend their first nights together.Both styles of art are made almost exclusively by women. Even its heritage tracing follows matrilineal succession, passed down from mothers to daughters. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.Sanjeev Kumar (IFS), principal chief conservator of forests and head of forest force for Jharkhand, has spent much of his career working alongside these villages. He offers a structural explanation for why this art form became a livelihood tool in the first place, rather than staying purely ceremonial.Jharkhand's rural economy runs largely on two crop cycles a year, he points out, which leaves long stretches when women in farming households have little steady work. Between the sowing and the harvest, there is a kind of enforced pause — and in that pause, an entire category of household income simply goes quiet.Painting, once confined strictly to festival and wedding seasons, has increasingly moved to fill exactly that gap, giving women a way to keep earning in the months the land itself has nothing to offer.It isn't only about income, in Kumar's telling. Starting in 2007, as Divisional Forest Officer in Dhanbad, he began organising folk art camps to give Sohrai a wider audience, drawing participants from across India and as far as Australia and Bangladesh. The camps followed him through later postings — Jamshedpur, Hazaribagh, and beyond — running until the pandemic forced them online, then resuming after. The same women who might once have sat out the off-season are now, through this ecosystem, training relatives, negotiating with buyers, and travelling to exhibitions. Kumar also frames the work as central to the state's eco-tourism ambitions.Sohrai-Khovar finally received Geographical Indication status in May 2020, reportedly approved in under nine months, unusually fast for a process that typically takes two to three years. The tag, granted by the Geographical Indication Registry in Chennai, formally recognises the art as unique to the Hazaribagh region, and gave it a marketing foothold it hadn't had before.The state took the recognition further. Hazaribagh became the first district in Jharkhand to commit to painting all its government buildings with Sohrai motifs — the chief minister's residence, the state secretariat, Ranchi's Birsa Munda Airport, railway stations across Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro, and Tata Nagar all now carry the same red-black-white language once found only on village walls. The art has travelled further still: Prime Minister Modi is reported to have gifted a Sohrai painting to President Putin, a livelihood project turned, however briefly, into an instrument of diplomacy.That visibility has translated into real, traceable livelihoods, in at least some cases. Local organisers connecting artists to buyers report dozens of women directly employed through their networks, hundreds more earning supplemental income in season. Cooperatives built specifically to give village women an alternative to farm labour have carried this work to dozens of international exhibitions across Europe and the US, and increasingly Canada, South Africa, and Japan. Trusts have gone further still — training programmes, small museums, free pigment, and the paperwork that eventually secured the GI tag itself.Not everyone close to this history agrees the shift toward livelihood has been a clean win. Gustav Imam draws a distinction between his father's original vision and the state's current one. Bulu Imam treated Sohrai as fine art from the start — building an exhibition circuit that ran shows in Australia and Europe. The government's livelihood framing, Gustav argues, risks something narrower: pay an artist per piece for a product and you've quietly converted her into daily-wage labour rather than treating her as an artist. He isn't against commercialisation itself; he simply thinks dignity has to come first, and that dignity requires recognition at the very top of the field, not just income at the bottom. Traditions like Madhubani, Warli, and Gond painting have each produced nationally awarded artists, Padma Shri recipients among them; Sohrai-Khovar has not, despite women keeping the tradition alive through real struggle and real limitation. Until a handful of individual artists receive that kind of recognition, he argues, younger painters have no one concrete to aspire to become.He also offers a blunt estimate on the schemes meant to help: of the artisans meant to benefit from government portals and initiatives like Mudra loans, perhaps 5 to 10 percent actually do, largely because many are semi-literate and simply can't navigate the registration process. The rest, in his account, remain outside the system entirely, not excluded by design, but by a bureaucracy that was never built with them in mind.Coal mining is often folded into this story as a single, simple threat, but the picture splits in two once you look closely. The Isco rock art site itself, the discovery that started everything, has not been destroyed. Dust from nearby mines has crept close and settled on it, but the site was declared a national monument around 2023. Other rock art caves in the region, more than a dozen now identified, remain safe largely because, in his words, no one knows about them, obscurity standing in for conservation.The villages are a different story. The North Karanpura coalfield sits beneath a large number of tribal villages across Hazaribagh, Ramgarh, and Chatra, and coal projects in the area have displaced multiple villages over the years, acquiring significant stretches of agricultural land in the process. Residents who've lost land describe rebuilding elsewhere, often some distance from where their families had always lived; local activists warn that further mining could displace still more. Bulu Imam's decades of opposition — intellectual rather than confrontational, built on letters to officials rather than protest, work that earned him the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2012 — was never really about the rock art surviving. It was about whether the people who kept painting around it would get to stay.There is another complication that has nothing to do with mining. Since 2018–19, a central housing scheme, the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Awas Yojana, has replaced mud-and-thatch homes across rural India with brick and cement — a genuine welfare improvement. But Sohrai and Khovar are painted on mud, and the same pigments don't take to cement the same way. One arm of government is quietly removing the canvas that another arm is simultaneously celebrating, not through malice, but through two policies that were never built with each other in mind.The most important complication was hinted at earlier. The market for Sohrai-Khovar remains thin, prices stay low relative to the labour involved, and no fixed floor price exists to stop buyers from talking artists down. Imam suggests that the district administration consider setting a standard pricing for the art to battle some aspects of the issue.The proposed fix, in Gustav's telling, isn't more schemes. It's status. He points to what happens when a piece lands somewhere with real institutional weight — a Sohrai painting, sold to the American ambassador during a visit to Kolkata, now hangs in a prominent hall at the US consulate.Contemporary Indian art by named painters routinely sells for crores; indigenous art too deserves a seat at that table. A tradition this old survives not just on income, but on being taken seriously by the people who could otherwise walk past it without a second look.The artisan finishes her peacock as the light starts to fade. Somewhere else in Hazaribagh, another woman is doing the same. Her red may no longer come from soil gathered by hand, but from a tube of paint bought at the market. The image on the wall is still recognisably Sohrai.For thousands of years, the art has adapted to changing walls, changing materials and changing lives. But preserving it may require more than putting its motifs on government buildings or selling its paintings to new markets. It may mean preserving the women who make it, the homes they paint and the communities that taught them how.The paintings began on cave walls, moved to mud homes and have now travelled to airports, exhibitions and diplomatic gifts. What happens next will depend on whether Sohrai-Khovar is treated simply as a product to be sold — or as a living tradition whose value lies in the people who keep painting it.
Article Summary: Sohrai and Khovar paintings are a unique and tribal style of art originating from caves of Jharkhand. It is one of the longest continuously practiced visual art traditions on the subcontinent. Traditionally it is classified as a Ma-Beti Parampara, with techniques passed down orally rather than written down.

Article Title: Turbulence-hit AI flight captain screening dope test 'not negative, sent for confirmatory test:' Govt
Article Text:
An Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet during cruise

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The pilots of Air India’s Aug 4 turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight were subjected to psychoactive substance (dope) screening test on arrival at the destination. The pilot-in-command or captain’s screening test report was not negative and has been sent for confirmatory tests, the aviation ministry said on Sunday. The ministry has classified the incident as a serious one which will now be probed by Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB). “Further action, as appropriate, will be taken based on the outcome of the investigation and confirmatory test results,” govt said.Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) rules stipulate that “in case the screening test is non-negative, the employee shall be immediately removed from the safety sensitive duty till a confirmatory report is received. In case of positive confirmatory test for the first time, the concerned employee shall be referred by the organisation” for de-addiction.The aviation ministry on Sunday said: “On Aug 4, Air India A320 (VT-EXO), operating flight AI 2379 from Phuket to Delhi, experienced a sudden loss of altitude of about 300 feet during cruise, following which the aircraft stabilised and subsequently landed safely at Delhi. During the occurrence, injuries were reported to a few passengers and cabin crew members on board.The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members comprising two pilots and six cabin crew. ”“As standard operating procedures following such an occurrence, both flight crew members underwent the prescribed psychoactive substance screening test. The screening test in respect of the pilot-in-command (PIC) indicated a result requiring confirmatory testing. Samples have accordingly been sent to the designated laboratory for confirmatory analysis, and the final report is awaited,” it added.Pending investigation, both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA. “The aviation ministry and DGCA remain firmly committed to maintaining the highest standards of aviation safety and ensuring that all such occurrences are thoroughly investigated and appropriate action is taken in accordance with the prescribed regulations and procedures,” the statement added.The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. People in the know say authorities are probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years. And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.
Article Summary: The pilot-in-command or captain’s screening test report was not negative and has been sent for confirmatory tests. The ministry has classified the incident as a serious one which will now be probed by Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau. Both pilots have been taken off flying duty by the DGCA.

NEW DELHI: Jharkhand chief minister Hemant Soren on Sunday urged youths protesting alleged irregularities in recruitment exams not to seek political patronage or allow their agitation to be politicised, saying dialogue, rather than batons, was the way to resolve issues."Samvad and not 'lathi-danda-bandook' (dialogue, not batons), can solve all problems," Soren said while addressing the Jharkhand Adivasi Mahotsav in Ranchi."Weapons are meant for enemies at the border. I promise the exam protesters that justice will be delivered with full transparency," the chief minister added.Soren further warned political parties and those with "political ambitions" against misleading the protesting youths through lies and misinformation."The stir should not be politicised; I warn those harbouring political ambitions against misguiding youths," he said."I urge youths not to seek political patronage (for their stir); justice is your right," Soren added.The chief minister said the concerns of the protesting students were also his own and assured them that those found guilty of irregularities would face strict action. "Those guilty of irregularities will face strict action.We caught theft, will deliver justice," he said.Soren also alleged that vested interests were attempting to disrupt democracy in Jharkhand and accused rival political parties, apparently referring to the BJP, of trying to mislead the state's youth.The protests over alleged irregularities in recruitment exams entered their 16th day on Sunday, with six demonstrators on an indefinite hunger strike.A sixth round of talks between the state government and the agitators was held at the state guest house in Ranchi.The protesters are seeking reforms in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC), along with an independent probe into the alleged irregularities. They have demanded either a CBI investigation or an inquiry by a panel of retired high court judges from outside the state.Soren also referred to the protests over the NEET exam paper leak at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, saying, "All saw how youths were tortured, had to face pellet guns, baton charges, and were declared traitors."
Article Summary: Jharkhand chief minister Hemant Soren urges youths not to seek political patronage or allow their agitation to be politicised. He says dialogue, rather than batons, is the way to resolve issues. The protests over alleged irregularities in recruitment exams entered their 16th day on Sunday.
